title: A General in a Yellow Slicker
author: Lexi Zotomayor
dek: A dusty bus stop by the Pasig River carries family habits, old landmarks, and the lingering story of a general who died a century before.
excerpt: Every conductor still hollers the name of a Civil War soldier at the foot of the ramp, long after the buses—and the history behind them—have moved on.
bodyText:
As far back as I can remember, it was simply the place where the buses stopped. I used to hear my father and his brothers and sisters speak of it at family gatherings—gatherings that came along often enough, since our family tree had grown as wide and many-branched as an old oak.

My father attended a college in Manila founded by Tomas Mapua, who had studied at Cornell. He and his older brother, Uncle Dante, would board the same bus bound for Plaza Lawton, though they always climbed down early along Vito Cruz Avenue. Years later, their younger sister, Aunt Daisy, rode that very same line, staying on until the end of the route.

Where the buses and jeepneys finally came to a halt, a traveler stood within sight of the reconstructed Manila Post Office, the Metropolitan Theater, the old *Puente Colgante*—which everyone called Quiapo Bridge—and City Hall,with its red clock tower.

Growing up, whenever my elders spoke of the city, their sentences were full of American names: Taft, Harrison,Lawton, Dewey, Dakota, Forbes. School was where I finally learned who those men were. In social studies, one of the first facts I picked up was that William Howard Taft had served as the first civil governor of the Philippines. After leaving the islands, he returned to the mainland, won the presidency, and years later became Chief Justice—the only man in American history to lead two separate branches of the federal government.

Then there was Lawton. Henry Ware Lawton was one of the most decorated American soldiers of his era, having earned the Medal of Honor during the Civil War and served in both the Spanish-American and Philippine-American wars.

On December 19, 1899, outside San Mateo, an officer told him that was no place for a general. Lawton went anyway. Tall and hard to miss, he wore a yellow slicker that hung around him like a gown and his famous white helmet. Near the edge of a low bluff above the river, a shot struck his left chest. He fell into the arms of his aide and ordnance officer and died within minutes. His troops took the town and brought his body inside. Word did not reach General Elwell Otis in Manila until eight that evening, and the papers took two days more to print the story. Longer still was the trip home to Washington, where he received a hero’s burial at Arlington.
Two sides exist to any story like that. To the Americans, Lawton had fought bravely to the end; to the Filipinos, his fall was a rare, galvanizing triumph in a resistance that would drag on for years.

![President Theodore Roosevelt dedicates Lawton Monument in 1907](/assets/uploads/cms/theodore_roosevelt_dedication_of_lawton_monument-_1907-05-30_-_dpla_-_acf6348107819c9db1805d0db157dd77-2.jpg "President Theodore Roosevelt led the dedication ceremony for the Lawton Monument in Indianapolis on May 30, 1907.")

Yet his name stuck to our corner of the world for generations. He died in 1899. A century later, his name still anchored a busy junction along the banks of the Pasig River. In my own youth, Lawton was simply the end of a three-hour bus ride from the province. I would step down onto the pavement with my nostrils blackened from exhaust and road dust,my hair stiffened by the humid wind, straight into the racket of honking jeepneys, cars, and buses. Around me rose the heavy grandeur of the Post Office, the clean classical lines of the Metropolitan Theater, and the steel span of Quiapo Bridge. Lawton was all of those things to me, and more.

Across more than a century, the place changed again and again. One habit stayed put. Whenever buses and jeepneys pull up before climbing the ramp over the Pasig River toward Santa Cruz, the driver or conductor still hollers, "Lawton! Lawton!" Without meaning to, we keep calling out the name of a general in a yellow slicker whose life was cut short by a Filipino rifle.
